solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Joke is supposed to be heard after hard time?

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by the ear, so we want a word that is spoken the same as the synonym

blocks.note: a pun is a play-on-words joke
taken as written
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
'supposed' (as in supposed to) is 'meant', said the same as the word ending -MENT

explanation.surface: A comedian's bad joke is deemed to deserve a spell in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supposed' is 'meant', heard as the ending -MENT; 'hard time' reads as one phrase meaning a prison stretch but splits into the abbreviation and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing time means serving a prison sentence, so time is used loosely for the penalty imposed on an offender.

clue.text: Put flags on quiet road

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
Ave is the abbreviation for avenue, a road

explanation.surface: Someone hangs bunting along a quiet street.
explanation.walkthrough: Flags here are flagstones, flat paving slabs, not banners waved on a quiet street.
explanation.definitionFit: Laying flagstones over ground is surfacing it with stone slabs, which is exactly what paving does.

clue.text: Surely bound to ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed or milled, so the letters are broken up and remade

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is certainly destined to be crushed or brought down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound to' looks like the phrase meaning 'certain to', which fits the definition's sense and hides that its letters are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are sentence adverbs expressing confident certainty, used interchangeably in speech to affirm that something is so.

clue.text: Clothing is bit of a hot potato?

blocks.clueFragment: Clothing is bit of a hot potato?
blocks.note: surface reading: a garment is something of a controversial subject
setter's reading: a baked potato fresh from the oven steams, and its skin has a culinary name that is also a garment

explanation.walkthrough: A 'hot potato' is an idiom for a touchy issue, but read literally it is a jacket potato still giving off steam.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a velvet lounging coat once worn by gentlemen while enjoying tobacco after dinner, so a garment.

clue.text: Mama perhaps sent back inside of horse to butcher

indicators.note: sending something back returns it the way it came, so its letters run in the opposite direction
being inside something means it surrounds you, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a mare is a female horse
Mama Cass was Cass Elliot of the Mamas and the Papas; 'perhaps' marks her as one example of a Mama

explanation.surface: A mother returned to the horse to slaughter it for meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Mama is not a mother but Mama Cass, the 1960s singer; her name reversed sits in the middle of MARE.
explanation.definitionFit: To butcher people is to kill them brutally and in large numbers, the verb sense of slaughter on a big scale.

clue.text: After introduction, write-up of Joan Miro half-ignored famous mother-in-law

indicators.note: only what comes after the opening is wanted, so the first letter is dropped
in a down entry, writing something up means it reads from bottom to top
ignoring half of a word means only half of its letters are kept

blocks.note: the name without its first letter
the first half of the painter's surname

explanation.surface: A review of a Joan Miró exhibition ignores half of it after the opening section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'write-up' looks like a review of the artist, but in a down clue it means reverse; only the trimmed Joan is reversed, then half of Miro follows.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Ruth, Naomi is the widow whose Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her, a famous biblical relationship.

clue.text: Flatter bit of orange included in juice

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small part of it, here its first letter
being included in something means being placed within it

blocks.note: sap is the juice of a plant
the opening letter of the fruit

explanation.surface: A piece of orange is added to a juice to improve it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' looks like a comparative adjective, as in more level, but it is the verb meaning to sweet-talk.
explanation.definitionFit: To soap someone, or soft-soap them, is to coax them with smooth compliments, an informal verb for buttering up.

clue.text: Work in Jerusalem, getting rid of first impression

indicators.note: getting rid of the first means the opening letter is thrown away

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
taken as written
Zion is a name for Jerusalem; without its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone working in Jerusalem tries to shake off a bad first impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first impression' reads as one phrase, but 'first' belongs with the deletion and 'impression' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An impression can be a view or belief formed about something, which is a synonym for a personal judgement.

clue.text: Are peelers running early screening?

indicators.note: running letters are in motion and loose, so they can end up in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; peelers is old British slang for police officers, after Sir Robert Peel

explanation.surface: Are the police dashing about doing early security checks on people?
explanation.walkthrough: Screening suggests police vetting, but it is a film showing; peelers is old British slang for police officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A film shown before its official launch date is an advance showing, put on ahead of general distribution.

clue.text: Cycling poet carrying eastern record

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves the front letter to the back
carrying something means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: Ovid was a Roman poet
E is the abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: A poet on a bicycle carries a record from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving the O of OVID to the end gives VIDO, which then holds E before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To video something is to capture it on camera, a verb synonym for taping or filming an event.

clue.text: Where you can see waves glisten around our realm, off and on

indicators.note: being off, then on, then off again means every other letter is kept
going around something means surrounding it

blocks.note: to shine is to glisten
the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Sunlit waves sparkle around the coast of our country now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the line where the sea meets land is the place to watch breakers.
explanation.definitionFit: The edge of a coast is where breakers roll in and are visible, a descriptive definition of the beach margin.

clue.text: Leave bass with tenor somehow losing verse complexity

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified manner, so the letters may be arranged in any way
losing something means it goes missing, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
V is the abbreviation for verse; this letter is the one removed

explanation.surface: Leaving out a verse simplifies a song for bass and tenor voices.
explanation.walkthrough: Take V out of LEAVE, then rearrange all the remaining letters of the three words; 'with' simply joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaborateness is the quality of being intricate and detailed, so it is a noun synonym for intricacy.

clue.text: Lennon song, absorbing at four past one in Paris routine

indicators.note: absorbing means soaking up and taking in, so one piece goes inside another
past means beyond or after, so this part comes later in the line

blocks.note: un is French for one
Imagine is John Lennon's 1971 song
taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A Lennon tune is played at four past one in a Parisian music-hall routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at four past one' looks like a time of day; 'past' really orders the pieces, putting the song after the French word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Routine as an adjective means ordinary and lacking originality, describing work done without creative flair or inventiveness.

clue.text: Son pilfering jewellery and dashing off

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to crib is to pilfer or copy
bling is slang for showy jewellery

explanation.surface: A son steals some jewellery and runs off with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dashing off' suggests running away from the theft, but it means writing something hastily.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash off a note is to write it quickly and carelessly, which is the same as hurried untidy writing.

clue.text: Mostly provide food – red sort

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: to cater is to provide food, without its last letter
gory means bloody, red with blood

explanation.surface: A host mostly serves up food, a red variety of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red sort' reads like a kind of wine or meat, but 'sort' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort is a kind or class of things grouped together, which is a direct noun synonym.

clue.text: Into dancing, plugging exercise tip for dancers

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places
plugging a gap means filling it, so this piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: PE is physical education, exercise at school
taken as written

explanation.surface: Keen on dancing, someone fits exercise in and picks up a tip for dancers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into dancing' reads as being keen on dance, but 'Into' is the fodder and 'tip' is the very end of the foot, not advice.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet, this means balancing on the extreme ends of the toes, so it is literally the point ballerinas stand on.

clue.text: Nobel laureate‘s duck/rabbit seen on television

blocks.note: to bob is to duck down quickly
Dylan is the laid-back rabbit in the children's TV show The Magic Roundabout

explanation.surface: A prizewinner's famous duck-rabbit illusion gets shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The duck/rabbit looks like the famous ambiguous drawing; instead it is a verb and a TV character. The Magic Roundabout is a long-running children's show popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer-songwriter won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016 for his song lyrics, making him a laureate.

clue.text: Part of trousers not initially wet in the morning

indicators.note: not initially means without its first letter

blocks.note: to rinse is to wet, minus its first letter
a.m. means in the morning

explanation.surface: Some trousers are only damp in the morning, not at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wet' is a verb here, the synonym being to rinse, which loses its R.
explanation.definitionFit: The inside leg seam running from crotch to hem is a component of every pair of trousers.

clue.text: Like some homes in Louisiana, perhaps likely to get gutted

indicators.note: perhaps marks the place as one example of a wider class
gutting removes the insides, so only the outside letters remain

blocks.note: Louisiana is one American state
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Houses in Louisiana are liable to be wrecked inside, perhaps by a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: A stately home is a grand country house in Britain, often open to the public.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand country houses in Britain are called stately homes, so the adjective describes that kind of residence.

clue.text: Lots of people drinking nearly expired syrup

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut
drinking means taking in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the masses are large numbers of people
old, as in past its date, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Crowds are drinking some syrup that is almost past its date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expired' suggests dead or out of date; OLD is the synonym, cut short and placed after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Molasses is the thick dark liquid left from refining sugar, a type of treacle-like sweetener.

clue.text: Spaniard’s agreed to eat what’s left over after roasting one’s fish dish

indicators.note: eating something takes it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: sí is Spanish for yes
ash is the residue of burning
I'm, 'one is' from the speaker's view

explanation.surface: A Spaniard agrees to eat the leftovers after a roast fish meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface teases with roasting, though this Japanese dish is never cooked; 'one's' stands for 'one is' said in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: Sashimi is a Japanese preparation of thinly sliced raw seafood, served without rice.

clue.text: Cooking place? Yes, with baked beans

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are changed into a new mix

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asked about a kitchen, someone confirms it comes with baked beans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking place' looks like a definition for a kitchen; 'Cooking' is the signal and 'baked' is fodder, not part of baked beans.
explanation.definitionFit: These are a variety of legume, cream-coloured with a dark spot, widely eaten in the American South.

clue.text: Year eight German trip abroad in this?

definitions.note: a descriptive definition: a vessel one might travel in

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year
acht is German for eight

explanation.surface: Year Eight pupils go on a school trip to Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: Year Eight is a British school year group for twelve-year-olds, so the surface suggests a school exchange; the question mark flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing boat is a craft people may voyage overseas in, hence the question-marked descriptive definition.

clue.text: Hill was captured

blocks.note: first meaning: a mountain or moor in northern England
second meaning: was taken by an enemy, as a city falls

explanation.walkthrough: In northern England, the hills of the Lake District are called fells.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a northern English noun for upland moor and the past tense of a verb used of besieged towns.

clue.text: Like dialect in Barking

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and crazy letters fall into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone describes the kind of accent spoken in Barking.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of east London, so the surface suggests a local accent; barking also means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Like as an adjective means alike or matching in every respect, as in 'of like mind'.

clue.text: Diet needed following final portion of ice cream

indicators.note: the final portion of a word is its last letter
following means coming after, so this piece is placed second

blocks.note: the closing letter
lite is a label for diet versions of foods

explanation.surface: A dieter needs to stop after the last bit of ice cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ice cream' reads as one dessert, but 'cream' is detached as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of society is its best and most select members, an idiom for the top group.

clue.text: Men discussed appearance

indicators.note: something discussed is talked over, so the word is judged by speech

blocks.note: a guise is an outward appearance

explanation.surface: Men talked about how they look.
explanation.walkthrough: A guise is an outward appearance, often an assumed one.
explanation.definitionFit: Guys is informal everyday slang for males, an exact plural synonym.

clue.text: Bears work without moving

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for a noun; it fits through 'at a standstill'

blocks.note: to stand something is to bear or tolerate it
to till is to work the soil

explanation.surface: Bears do their work while staying perfectly still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals, but it is the verb to tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at a halt has come to a complete stop, a state of no motion at all.
